title: Can a raise shrink your take-home?
hook: The raise pushes you into the 30% bracket. Could you end up with less?

knows: income tax is a percentage of pay
doesNotKnow: that a higher bracket's rate applies only to the income above its threshold

misconception: A raise that pushes me into a higher bracket can leave me with less take-home.
objective: The learner can compute take-home pay under two brackets and explain that the higher rate taxes only the dollars above the line, so more pay means more take-home.

claims.text: With 10% on the first $20,000 and 30% above, $19,000 of pay is taxed $1,900, leaving $17,100.
$21,000 of pay is taxed $2,300 ($2,000 + $300), leaving $18,700: take-home rises by $1,600.
In this system each extra dollar above $20,000 keeps 70 cents, so more pay always means more take-home.
claims.source: d(takeHome)/d(pay) = 0.9 below 20,000 and 0.7 above, both positive.

claims.text: A higher bracket's rate applies only to the dollars above its threshold.
claims.source: Marginal vs average tax rate in a progressive bracket system (N. G. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 12 'The Design of the Tax System', marginal and average tax rates).

claims.text: The brackets are invented, not any country's, and the model ignores credits and other taxes.
claims.source: Stage chip 'Made-up tax'; reveal's last line. (Real systems can have benefit phase-outs that are not modelled here.)

recall.question: A tax is 20% on income up to $50,000 and 40% above. Someone's pay rises from $49,000 to $51,000. Roughly how much of the $2,000 raise do they keep?
options: None: the whole income is now taxed at 40%
recall.why: The first $1,000 of the raise is taxed 20% (keep $800), the next $1,000 at 40% (keep $600). Only dollars above the line pay the higher rate.
